newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIAN RENAULT PLANT SPUTTERS TO WORK.
newsitem.headline: BELGIAN RENAULT PLANT SPUTTERS TO WORK.

text.p: Workers at the doomed Renault SA plant near Brussels resumed work on Monday after a six-week strike, but only part of the 3,100 strong workforce returned and production got off to a slow start.

Employees at the Vilvoorde plant, which the French car maker is determined to close down, had made only 120 cars by midday, falling far short of management's target. Before the strike Renault Industrie Belgique made 820 cars a day.
"Of course people are demotivated," metal workers union leader Karel Gacoms said.

Belgian radio said workers at the plant's painting and assembly sections in particular had been loathe to resume production and were debating union strategy, thus holding up the assembly line and preventing other employees from working.
In a referendum last Thursday on union tactics in the struggle to prevent the shutdown, over sixty-eight percent of the workers were in favour of a resumption.
Gacoms noted this meant about a third of the workers had wanted to continue the strike until the bitter end or had lost interest in efforts to preserve their jobs.

Renault workers continued to occupy the plant's car park on Monday, holding billions of francs worth of finished cars as bargaining chips in any talks with management. They also vowed to take further action to try and preserve their jobs.
Gacoms said staff had been upset by remarks by Renault chief executive officer Louis Schweitzer, who said on Sunday there was no question of overturning the decision to close down the plant.
The controversial July closure could be put off by a few weeks or months, depending on negotiations with unions, Schweitzer told RTL radio.
"That is a provocation one day before the resumption of work...that does little to calm people," Gacoms said.
A majority of workers at Renault Vilvoorde had voted to return to work after winning moral victories over the partially state owned car group in the courts.

Claiming Renault's thunderbolt decision in February broke Belgian, French and European Union labour laws since the company failed to inform and consult workers adequately, unions took the car maker to court in France and Belgium.
Judges in both countries ordered Renault to play it by the book, effectively reversing the decision to shut down Vilvoorde.

Analysts said the unions' move to return to work was part of a strategy to begin lengthy negotiations about the terms and conditions of the closure of the profitable plant, which Renault says is needed to cut overcapacity and rising costs.
The company is also cutting nearly 2,800 jobs in France.

After the court rulings, which Renault has said it is appealing, unions decided to take legal action to force the company to pay out wages to the workers for the duration of the strike since formally they had remained on the Renault payroll.

It is unclear how long any talks on the terms and conditions could take, but it is certain unions will draw them out as long as possible. The court appeals could take until the end of April, and only then would the formal closure procedure start.
